\chapter{What Pleases Me}
\label{ch:sa-what-pleases-me}
\hlchaptermodality{58}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what I like in Sanskrit, putting myself in the dative and the thing I like in the nominative as the subject.}

Complete SA-R58-likes and say all three frames, naming the subject of each.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[mahyam]{\sk{मह्यम्} (mahyam) — to me, for me}

\label{lesson:SA-C58-mahyam}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\sk{अहम्}} and what it means. Then recall \textbf{\sk{पुनर्दर्शनाय}} — what did its \textbf{-\sk{आय}} ending do?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{मह्यम्}}
\textbf{\sk{मह्यम्}} (\emph{mahyam}) — \textquotedblleft{}to me, for me\textquotedblright{}.

You have used the dative case once already, without a pronoun in it. \textbf{\sk{पुनर्दर्शनाय}} — \emph{for seeing again}, your first farewell — was a noun in the dative, and the ending said \textquotedblleft{}this is what it is \textbf{for}\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{मह्यम्}} is that same case, on \textbf{\sk{अहम्}}. \emph{I} becomes \emph{to me}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{अहम्}} — I, the one doing
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{मह्यम्}} — to me, the one it is done for
\end{quote}

The word looks less like \textbf{\sk{अहम्}} than you might expect, and that is not irregularity for its own sake: \textbf{\sk{अहम्}} and \textbf{\sk{मह्यम्}} come from two different ancient stems that the language pressed into one pronoun. English does exactly the same — \emph{I} and \emph{me} share no letters either, for the same reason.

On its own \textbf{\sk{मह्यम्}} is not much. In the next lesson it becomes the whole point, because Sanskrit's ordinary way of saying that you like something puts \textbf{you} in this case and the thing you like in the subject.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The word for the person something is done to or for.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{aham}, then \emph{mahyam}
  \item \emph{Say it:} which of the two is the subject, and which is the one receiving
  \item \emph{Recall:} the chapter-4 word whose ending was the same case
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\sk{मह्यम्}}, then say what it means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\sk{मह्यम्}} mean, and what case is it? (\textquotedblleft{}To me\textquotedblright{}, the dative.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rocate]{\sk{रोचते} (rocate) — is pleasing to}

\label{lesson:SA-C58-rocate}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\sk{मह्यम्}}, and say what case it is in.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the thing you like is the subject}]
Sanskrit has no verb that means \textquotedblleft{}to like\textquotedblright{} with the liker as its subject. It says something else, and once you see the shape it is easy:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{मह्यं} \sk{फलं} \sk{रोचते}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{mahyaṁ phalaṁ rocate}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{the fruit is pleasing to me} — that is, \textbf{I like the fruit}
\end{quote}

Look at what is doing what:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{case} & \textbf{job} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\sk{मह्यम्}} & dative & the person who does the liking \\
\textbf{\sk{फलम्}} & nominative & the thing liked — and the SUBJECT \\
\textbf{\sk{रोचते}} & verb & agrees with the fruit, not with me \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The verb agrees with the thing you like.} If two things pleased you, the verb would be plural, and \textbf{\sk{मह्यम्}} would not change at all. The liker is never the subject of this sentence.

If you have met Spanish, you have met this exact shape: \emph{me gusta la fruta} — the fruit pleases me. Two unrelated branches of Indo-European settled on the same answer, which is a good sign that the English way round is the odd one.

And the root is worth a moment. \textbf{\sk{रुच्}} means \textquotedblleft{}to shine\textquotedblright{}. \emph{The fruit shines for me} is what the sentence originally said. The same root gives Latin \emph{lūx}, \textquotedblleft{}light\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{lūcēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to shine\textquotedblright{} — and through Latin it gives English \emph{lucid} and \emph{translucent}. Liking something, in Sanskrit, is that thing lighting up for you.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A way to say what you like, with the grammar the language actually uses.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mahyaṁ phalaṁ rocate}
  \item \emph{Say it:} which word the verb agrees with
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\sk{मह्यं} \sk{फलं} \sk{रोचते}}, then say what it means in ordinary English
  \item \emph{Contrast:} English makes the liker the subject; Sanskrit makes the thing liked the subject
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
In \textbf{\sk{मह्यं} \sk{फलं} \sk{रोचते}}, who is the subject? (The fruit.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I like the fruit\textquotedblright{} in Sanskrit.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mahyaṁ … rocate]{\sk{मह्यं} … \sk{रोचते} — the liking frame, reviewed}

\label{lesson:SA-R58-likes}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}I like the fruit\textquotedblright{} in Sanskrit, and name the subject of the sentence you said.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three sentences about what a person is able to do, wants to do, and likes — and two of the three share a shape while the third breaks it deliberately.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\sk{बालः} \sk{पठितुम्} \sk{शक्नोति}} — the boy \textbf{can} read
  \item \textbf{\sk{बालः} \sk{पठितुम्} \sk{इच्छति}} — the boy \textbf{wants to} read
  \item \textbf{\sk{मह्यं} \sk{फलं} \sk{रोचते}} — I \textbf{like} the fruit
\end{itemize}

The first two put the person in the nominative and an infinitive before the verb. The third puts the person in the \textbf{dative} and makes the liked thing the subject.

That is not an inconsistency to be smoothed over — it is the fact about Sanskrit worth carrying out of this chapter. Ability and desire belong to the person. Pleasing is something the \textbf{thing} does.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bālaḥ paṭhitum śaknoti}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bālaḥ paṭhitum icchati}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mahyaṁ phalaṁ rocate}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} name which of the three puts the person in the dative
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say all three sentences, and for each one name who or what the subject is.
\end{tcolorbox}
